title: EPA Repeals Pollution Limits on Power Plants
summary:
Have you ever seen smoke rising from a power plant and wondered where it goes? That smoke contains carbon dioxide — a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere and is the main driver of global warming. On Monday, the Trump administration announced it is removing limits on how much of that gas power plants can release.

The head of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Lee Zeldin, called it the largest deregulatory action in U.S. power sector history. The rules being eliminated were finalized during the Biden administration. They required existing coal plants and new natural gas plants to significantly reduce their carbon dioxide pollution starting in the 2030s.

Power plants are the second-largest source of planet-heating carbon dioxide in the U.S., behind transportation. At a press conference in Houston, where the U.S. is hosting the G20 Energy Summit, Zeldin said that previous efforts to cut pollution led to higher energy prices and prevented the country from reaching its full energy potential. "The days of Biden and Obama working to destroy natural gas and coal are over," he said.

Environmental groups disagree strongly. "These rules are really important, not just for our climate, but also to protect public health from the dangers of local air pollution," said Gudrun Thompson, a senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center. They plan to challenge the decision in court.

Last month was the hottest ever recorded globally. Michael Gerrard, a law professor at Columbia University, said, "2026 is shaping up to be the warmest year in recorded history, and we ain't seen nothing yet."
why_it_matters: The air you breathe and the heat you feel on the playground are both connected to this decision — with fewer pollution limits, the air could get dirtier and the planet warmer, which affects kids' health and the world they will grow up in.

background_read: The Environmental Protection Agency (the U.S. government group that makes rules to keep air and water clean) is in charge of these pollution limits.
In 2015, countries around the world signed the Paris Agreement, a promise to work together to slow global warming.
In the United States, coal power plants have been closing for years as natural gas and clean energy like wind and solar have become cheaper.
Article_Structure: WHO: The Trump administration and EPA head Lee Zeldin, against environmental groups such as the Southern Environmental Law Center and law professor Michael Gerrard.
WHAT: The EPA announced it is removing limits on how much carbon dioxide power plants may release — rules that were finalized under President Biden and were set to start in the 2030s.
WHERE: Announced at a press conference in Houston, where the U.S. is hosting the G20 Energy Summit.
WHY: Power plants are the second-biggest source of planet-heating carbon dioxide in the U.S., and last month was the hottest month ever recorded worldwide.

perspectives.description: They argue that the old rules raised energy prices and held the country back, so removing them means cheaper electricity and more energy for everyone.
They say the limits protect people's lungs and the climate, especially in neighborhoods near power plants, and they plan to fight the change in court.
They point out that no matter what the rules say, the planet keeps heating up — the hottest month ever recorded just happened, and researchers warn worse is coming.
